There is a lot of focus on AI-aided discoveries in quantitative fields, but they can go beyond that, too:

Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to look at an anonymous 1808 sketchbook at Yale and it found the author, an obscure French aristocrat. https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical

Thing I am hearing from a number of big firms, from manufacturers to financial services: we have scattered teams of 2-3 people using AI that are doing the work of dozens of folks in a fraction of the time, creating large-scale management fights over the implications and politics.

@emollick In addition to putting forth the John Galt narrative about these heroic teams doing the work of hundreds, we should also entertain the possibility that they are making a hash of things in these other domains where they are relying on canned expertise rather than deep knowledge.
From the author

quoted_tweet.author: Mark Humphries
quoted_tweet.text:
In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the  process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history.

You can read the full post here:

https://generativehistory.substack.com/p/gpt-62-astra-solves-a-historical

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.

With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found.

I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history.

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. The itinerary also aligned perfectly with the few dated drawings in the book. But there was actually the type of conclusive evidence we rarely get as historians: on 18 June 1808, after Chabot’s canoe reached Fort St. Joseph, he wrote “I took a sketch” before describing the exact view of the fort depicted in a matching drawing.

The journal itself is also a major find. It had been mentioned once in a dissertation footnote, but in a completely different area of history and is unknown to fur trade or Canadian historians. It’s long and detailed, covering some 162 notebook pages which makes this a significant new document to my field. Attached to the journal was another trove of documents too: excerpts from long-destroyed North West Company papers, journals, and letters. Again, this almost never happens. Both finds equally surprised the other leading experts I consulted.

Although we can construct a coherent narrative in hindsight, I cannot emphasize enough how exceedingly difficult this sort of thinking and recall is for humans. Unlike a human, Astra was able to tackle the problem from both ends at once: working forward from the scant facts of the 1808 journey pictured in the sketchbook and backwards from the immense number of surviving facts about 1808 British North America in general.

While we can technically explain Astra’s path to this find as a product of enhanced search capabilities, it conducted the investigation from end to end. I basically acted as the research assistant, restricting copies of the paper documents it needed.

To my mind, this puts historians in a similar position as the mathematicians found themselves about eleven months ago, when LLMs started to solve the first Erdős problems. Over the past year, we’ve watched these same models go from learning to read handwriting, to beginning to think historically, to mastering the undergraduate essay, and finally to making small but real contributions to human knowledge more or less autonomously.

The trajectory seems clear.

You can now let Claude review your pull requests and approve the safe ones. Before you turn it on, write the one file that decides what it's allowed to merge.

Anthropic launched Claude Ship yesterday. 10,000 people saved the launch post in a day.

What it does:
→ You run /ship in Claude Code, in the terminal or the desktop app
→ Claude opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks
→ It approves what your team's policy allows. Your permissions and branch rules still decide what merges
→ On Team and Enterprise, admins can turn it on for a whole repo, with the policy living in the repo like a smarter CODEOWNERS file

The review isn't the risky part. The policy is. If nobody writes down what Claude may approve alone, "what the policy allows" becomes whatever the default allows.

3 prompts to set it up before your first /ship:

Prompt 1: Write the approval policy
"Read this repo: the folder structure, CODEOWNERS, CI config and the last 20 merged PRs. Draft an approval policy in three sections. Claude may approve alone: changes like [docs, tests, copy, patch-level dependency bumps]. Needs a human: anything touching [auth, payments, database migrations, infra, public APIs]. Never merge: changes that delete data, edit secrets or turn off a check. For each rule, show one real PR from the history it would have caught. Flag any folder that fits no section."

Prompt 2: Pre-ship self-check
"Before I run /ship, review my diff as the reviewer who gets blamed if this breaks production. List what changed, what could break, which tests prove it works, and anything I changed that the PR description doesn't mention. If a change that matters has no test, write the test first."

Prompt 3: Friday audit
"List every PR Claude approved this week. For each one: what it changed, which policy rule allowed it, and whether a human reviewer would have asked for changes. Suggest one rule to tighten and one to relax, with the PR that proves each."

Start strict. Loosen the policy after a week of audits, not before.

Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.

SpaceX has agreed to forgo $738 million in U.S. federal broadband subsidies and instead provide free @Starlink hardware to eligible American households.

NTIA: "To ensure that no consumer at a Covered BSL is left behind, the provider (SpaceX) will serve the covered BSLs as this agreement provides. This includes providing customer premises equipment at no cost to new subscribers, so that households at covered BSL do not face the upfront equipment costs. Additionally, the provider’s broadband service will be subject to the same delivery timelines and performance testing requirements applicable to all recipients of BEAD funds."

Under the new agreement, SpaceX would:
• Provide free Starlink hardware to eligible households.
• Guarantee minimum download speeds of 100 Mbps and upload speeds of 20 Mbps.
• Offer a low-cost monthly internet plan.
• Commit to providing service for 10 years.
• Continue to comply with federal performance testing requirements.

The agreement will save American taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars while accelerating high-speed internet access in underserved rural communities.

In exchange, SpaceX would be exempt from most BEAD-related financial audits, procurement requirements and administrative reporting, while remaining subject to network performance testing.

Alpöge 回应黎曼猜想证明争议：“25万页文档”是开玩笑话，Lean 代码写的很烂但证明成立

用 Claude 证明黎曼猜想的 Anthropic 数学家 Levent Alpöge，在 X 上发了一篇《我做过的蠢事》，正面回应这几天的争议。

先说结论：证明本身没有问题。1700 万行代码的正确性已获官方核查通过，他认错的是“表述开玩笑”和“代码太乱”，并点出了这次证明真正值得思考的数学意义。

1. 辟谣与认错：他澄清了三件事

• “25万页文档”是个玩笑：他不想给黎曼猜想配一份 AI 糊出来的注水说明，又觉得自己写不出可读版本，索性拿 Lean 往夸张了凑字数自娱自乐，甚至在定理开头写“因为实数是全序的，所以不等于 1/2 时要么大于 1/2 要么小于 1/2”，本以为这么荒诞的废话一眼就能看出是反讽，结果被媒体和学界全盘当真。

他为此道歉，感叹终于明白陶哲轩为什么劝人“别在论文里开玩笑”。（他还顺带自嘲：之前做四维杨-米尔斯存在性攒了 6 万页 AI 草稿，结果审核委员会一句“要看 Lean”，让他觉得啃草稿纯属浪费时间。）

• 代码确实“满是垃圾”，但能编译：他承认 1700 万行 Lean 代码里有很多自己“瞎冲（yolo）”试出来的弯路和冗余，最终绝大部分可能都用不上，只是清理起来莫名困难，所有对代码质量的批评他全盘接受。

• 承认拖延前科：同行 Scott Armstrong 看穿了他，他学生时代就有定理拖了快十年才整理成文，这次他承诺会更负责地把证明精简出来。

2. 核心事实：代码再丑，证明依然成立

在形式化验证里，“不好读”和“对不对”是两件事：

1). Lean 官方（Lean FRO）与 Mathlib 已联合认证：定理陈述没有偷换概念，几十人独立编译结果完全一致，证明成立。

2) MIT 数学家 Andrew Sutherland 独立跑完核查：证明只用到了 Lean 的三条标准公理，没有作弊。

3. 最有启发的一点：为什么证出来了还不满意？

Alpöge 说，他在声明里漏掉了自己真正想强调的重点：

这种又长又杂的暴力论证本身只是“原材料”，真正的目的是帮数学家反推出“正确的定义”。

几十年前，Weil 和 Deligne 干净利落地证明了有限域曲线上的“简化版黎曼猜想”，靠的是一套成熟的几何工具；但在普通整数（数域）上，数学界至今找不到对应的核心结构（即他说的缺一个“H¹ 对象”）。

他的原话：“黎曼猜想本该很简单。任何真正的困难都说明，我们现在的数学框架还很蠢。”

4. 留给数学界的新局面

这次事件把数学推到了一个前所未有的分水岭：机器已经确认“它是对的”，但人类还不知道“它为什么对”。

陶哲轩初步浏览后指出，这份证明似乎动用了现代朗兰兹纲领和算术几何的全部武器；也有数学家认为：Lean 代码回答不了数学最关心的“为什么”。

按照克雷研究所百万美元奖金的规则，证明仍需在期刊正式发表满两年并获学界共识。

text: 在葬礼上播放用 AI 生成的逝者“驾鹤西去”视频

LlamaIndex 公开两款文档解析模型：40 亿参数的 OCRia-1 用 GPU 跑复杂表格和图表，810 万参数的 nano 用 CPU 跑日常文档，营收或融资超 200 万美元的公司商用要买授权

LlamaIndex 先后发了两款把 PDF 和扫描件转成 Markdown 的模型。10 月 22 日发的 OCRia-1 有 40 亿参数，要用 GPU，专门对付复杂表格、图表和公式，当天就用到了 LlamaParse 云服务里。11 月 23 日发的 OCRia-nano-1 只有 810 万参数，在普通 CPU 上跑，负责大量日常文档。

两款的权重 11 月 23 日都放上了 Hugging Face。个人、研究和小公司可以免费用，年营收或累计融资超过 200 万美元的公司拿来做业务，要找 LlamaIndex 另买授权。

【OCRia-1：表格、图表、格式】

OCRia-1 基于阿里的 Qwen3.5-4B，用约 10 万页文档做了监督微调和强化学习。在 LlamaIndex 自家的 ParseBench 上（第一版，文字、格式、表格、图表四项平均），它得 87.4 分，比第二名 LightOnOCR-3-4B 的 75.3 高 12.1 分。

差距最大的是图表。它会把柱状图、折线图读成一张数据表，每个数字放在对应的系列和标签下，这一项 85.1 分，第二名 66.1。上标、下标、删除线、勾选框这些格式也会保留，公式写成 LaTeX，手写公式也能认，格式这一项 83.4 分，第二名 67.9。

换到三个外部机构做的基准，它在表格上还是第一，但领先不多：olmOCR-bench 表格 92.9 对 92.1，PulseBench-Tab 84.1 对 82.4，fr-bench-pdf2md 的长表格 83.2 对 80.6。博客的对比只列了 35B 以下的模型，模型页补上了 350 亿参数的 Infinity-Parser2-Pro，olmOCR-bench 总分 83.5 对 83.2，基本打平。在新版 ParseBench-2 的完整排行榜上，它在开放权重模型里第一，算上商业 API 和前沿大模型排第七。

速度要看在哪跑。LlamaParse 用的是量化加推测解码的优化版，一张 B200 显卡上单个请求每秒解码约 4700 个 Token，64 个请求并发每秒处理 10.2 页。Hugging Face 上放的是没优化的原始权重，约 10GB，用标准 vLLM 跑大约慢 9 倍。

【OCRia-nano-1：CPU 上的日常款】

nano 由七个小模型组成：找文字行、判断文字类型（拉丁字母、中日韩、阿拉伯和希伯来文，以及约 17 种其他文字）、四个识别器分别认字，再由一个 427 万参数的表格和版面模型还原结构。电子版 PDF 自带文字的部分直接读，只有扫描件和图片里的字才动用识别。

在 ParseBench-2 上，nano 总分 59.2，表格 59.5。同一台 16 核机器上，Datalab 家的两款同类 CPU 工具 Indra 是 55.1、Marker 是 52.5，LiteParse 原来默认的 Tesseract 配置是 48.7。单核平均每页 426 毫秒，16 核并行每秒 27.8 页，是 Tesseract 配置的 2 倍。

同一基准上 OCRia-1 在 LlamaParse 里是 87.0 分，nano 大约是它的三分之二。nano 没有图表模型，图表原样留成图片，这一项只有 3.1 分；扫描件里的公式也认不出来。官方也没单独公布 nano 的中文成绩。

【怎么用】

OCRia-1 最省事的用法是 LlamaParse，按页扣积分，每月送 1 万积分。LlamaIndex 说换上 OCRia-1 后价格不变，但没说它对应哪一档。想自己部署，要有 NVIDIA 显卡，用 vLLM 或 Transformers 加载。

nano 跑在 LlamaIndex 的开源本地解析工具 LiteParse 里：

pip install liteparse
lit models pull ocria-nano
lit parse doc.pdf --format markdown

模型加运行库一共下载 60 到 75MB，拉下来以后 LiteParse 默认就改用它。也支持 Node.js 和浏览器。

【能不能商用】

两款权重的许可证条款一样，都是 LlamaIndex 在 Open RAIL-M 基础上改的：个人使用、研究、评测免费；上一年营收和累计融资都不超过 200 万美元的组织，可以免费商用。超过任一门槛，或者拿它做跟 LlamaParse 竞争的文档解析服务（不论公司大小），都要买授权。许可证还禁止用它们的输出训练类似的模型。LiteParse 本身是 Apache 2.0，不受这些限制。

以上跑分都是 LlamaIndex 自己测的，ParseBench 也是 LlamaIndex 做的基准；三个外部基准的题库是别家做的，分数也是 LlamaIndex 自己跑、自己整理的，还没有第三方复现。nano 的博客开头说它比 Tesseract 快“2 到 5 倍以上”，技术报告里对 Tesseract 的数字是吞吐 2 倍、单页平均约 1.8 倍。

OCRia-1 博客：https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/parse-ocria-1
OCRia-1 模型与许可证：https://huggingface.co/llamaindex/OCRia-1
OCRia-nano-1 博客：https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/introducing-ocria-nano-1
OCRia-nano-1 模型与许可证：https://huggingface.co/llamaindex/OCRia-nano-1

Today we are open-sourcing the weights to OCRia-1, our flagship 4B VLM for document OCR 🔥

This is our SECOND open-weight release in two days (we just launched OCRia-nano-1 yesterday!!).

OCRia-1 is on the pareto curve of accuracy and cost relative to other 4B models on multiple benchmarks: ParseBench, olmOCR-bench (tables), PulseBench-Tab, and fr-bench-pdf2md. It is an extremely general purpose model that can parse even the most complex document types, including complex tables/charts/formatting/layout.

We’re releasing the weights to help advance open research around OCR, on both @huggingface  🤗 and @ollama  🦙

If you want to use it in prod, come talk to us. If you want to use the latest SOTA of the OCRia model family, tuned for production, check out LlamaParse!

Release on @huggingface : https://huggingface.co/llamaindex/OCRia-1

Release on @ollama: https://ollama.com/llamaindex/ocria-1

LlamaParse: https://llamaparse.ai/

@kirso_ We often land in finance. Also just the first of many AI Transformation Office Hours.

Today @OpenAI and @Cisco jointly announced a new Opensource Linux runtime that was imagined from the ground up for the agentic era. As attacks happen at machine scale, defenses can no longer be at human scale alone. They must also be at machine scale. 

There are three things that are worth mentioning: 

1. AI models are getting very good at finding security flaws. 

2. Attackers are getting better and faster at exploiting these flaws

3. The agents we are developing in our enterprises are a new risk vector. 

These traps are only exacerbated by the speed of AI. The defenders window is shrinking. 

Adversaries don’t wait for the patch to be applied. They are getting very good at exploiting minutes after the vuln is announced. Patching is hard and time consuming. In order to expand the defender’s window, mitigation shields that don’t stop all traffic. but protect the vulnerability attack chain can help organizations respond quickly to the threats without putting resilience at risk. 

This is the beginning of a new security architecture that helps defend humanity against adversarial attacks by agent swarms in an agent native way. 

The reason we decided to have this very important body of innovation as an opensource initiative is because the true enemy is the adversary and we have to as a community share meaningful inventions with everyone to build upon to achieve maximum impact. 

Thanks to @gdb and the entire @OpenAI team for advancing our partnership for the safety and security of critical infrastructure. 

Also a huge thanks to @danwendlandt, @tgraf__ and the @isovalent team for making eBPF agent native. You truly ROCK! 

We hope to see many more contributors join the effort. 

My blog link: https://blogs.cisco.com/news/expanding-the-defenders-window-with-self-defending-infrastructure

Announcing Epochal! ✨

We believe the best measure of intelligence is the ability to predict the future. Doing so requires learning about the past and constantly working to be less wrong.

Today's AI has read almost everything and lived through almost nothing. It learns from the internet all at once, already knowing how each story ends. 

We want it to live through thousands of yesterdays instead, one day at a time, the way people do.

So, we built Epochal Time Portal, the first true point-in-time environment with trillions of pages spanning 30 years of history, where agents can browse the Internet as it existed on a past date.
@Baxate @kernelcdub Sick pod
@nvidia @RedHat @kernelcdub 🔥
@epochal Congrats!

For everyone complaining that all the ideas in AI are taken, or that AI has nowhere to grow from here, please realize:

The applications for AI are infinite. Meaning the breadth of information that may matter to agents is infinite. 

Records of history for agents is a genius concept.

Anthropic just published a chart that visualizes what I've been saying for a year now. 
- A chatbot doesn't move the needle.
- Point solution AI doesn't move the needle.  
- If you want to WIN in AI, you HAVE to go deep. 

Look at all the use cases on the bottom left of the chart: "slide decks", "ad hoc data analysis", "competitive analysis"… All of them required individuals to change their habits but offered almost no value.

Compare that to the top right: "document review", "frontline support agents", "coding agents"… All of them required re-engineering the processes.

So what does it take to get from the bottom left to the top right?
- Map the current process meticulously, including exceptions (what's in the SOP and what's in the system logs are often very different)
- Agree with the business on what KPI the new process will measure (time, revenue minus token cost, or risk), just one
- Re-engineer the process to reduce the number of steps, say from 15 to 5, four of which will be done by AI
- Build AI agents that interact with the systems you already have (SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow, etc.), no new systems to learn
- Get a C-suite sponsor for the project. If you don't have someone at that level, you won't be able to eliminate steps, merge teams, or change KPIs, which will force you to automate the existing process (good luck with that)
- Have the people who will be running the new process own the AI agents, be responsible for handling exceptions, and improve them over time

And that last point is how you deal with Ethan's second point. People are going to fight changes that are being done to them, but they're going to participate in changes they're taking ownership of.

Elon Musk on the maniacal sense of urgency behind his companies:

"I'm constantly addressing the limiting factor."

"I generally try to aim for a deadline that I at least think is at the 50th percentile. So it's not like an impossible deadline, but it's the most aggressive deadline I can think of that could be achieved with 50% probability. Which means that it'll be late half the time."

"A maniacal sense of urgency is a very big deal. You want to have an aggressive schedule. And then you want to figure out what the limiting factor is at any point in time and help the team address that limiting factor."

Ben Horowitz says a16z copied CAA's model almost exactly:

"You had talent agents, and they would get you jobs, and they all operated independently of each other. And all the winnings went to the ones who had been around, because if you're a great actress, are you going to go to William Morris, who you've heard of, or some new agent?"

"That all changed when Michael Ovitz started a firm called CAA, and he introduced this new model of, 'You're not just getting an agent, you're getting a platform.' And we, because we knew Michael, we kind of copied the CAA design almost exactly and applied it to venture capital."
